Photo taken in Hattiesburg, MS during an EPA Brownfield Site Assessment “tank yank.”




I’m a social scientist, resilience researcher, and data nerd interested in what happens when environmental risk meets the places people actually live.
My work combines social science, spatial analysis, and community resilience. I use R, GIS, and real-world data to study flooding, housing, insurance, and vulnerability, and turn that information into something communities can actually use.
I earned my Ph.D. in Sociology studying inequities in disaster impacts and recovery, and now work on applied resilience projects across coastal Mississippi. At the heart of my work is a love for using data to answer questions that matter to real places and real people.

title: Hurrican Ida: Wind & Storm Surge Attribution Analysis
text:
This interdisciplinary project with LSU, the National Center for Atmospheric Research, and The Water Institute examined Hurricane Ida’s impacts under changing climate conditions.
My role was to integrate modeled wind and storm-surge damage estimates with demographic data and to analyze the distribution of climate change attributable impacts across different populations and communities.

title: Hurrican Ida: Wind & Storm Surge Attribution Analysis
text:
Research Significance
By connecting physical climate attribution modeling with social and demographic data, this research contributes to understanding not only how climate change intensifies disaster impacts, but also how those additional damages are distributed across communities.
The findings can inform discussions of climate-related inequality, disaster vulnerability, and the equitable allocation of adaptation and recovery resources.
Code & Reproducibility: View Project on GitHub.

title: Climate Change & Federal Aid Dispersements
text:
Overview
This was an interdisciplinary effort to assess the relationship between climate change attributable damages and federal disaster assistance.
I integrated modeled flood damages with FEMA NFIP paid claims and Individual Assistance payouts, applied spatial lag regression models to estimate both direct and spatial spillover effects of attributable damages, and created maps to visualize the relationship.
Results indicate that while both attributable and non-attributable flood damages were associated with federal aid, climate change attributable damages generally had larger effect sizes, particularly for Individual Assistance.

title: Bay St. Louis | CRS Activity 510
text:
Overview
This ongoing project supports the City of Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, in developing floodplain management planning documents under FEMA’s Community Rating System (CRS) Activity 510.
The project integrates flood hazard, property, infrastructure, and insurance data to characterize the city’s exposure to multiple flooding hazards and inform local flood mitigation priorities. Additional analysis of historical shoreline change examines patterns of coastal erosion and accretion to better understand changes along the city’s waterfront.




My Role & Contributions
Community Engagement & Planning

Developed flood risk maps and spatial analyses, contributed to planning documents, and participated in stakeholder engagement to support local floodplain management strategies.

Floodplain Management Plan

Multi-Hazard Exposure Assessment: Mapped storm surge, high-tide flooding, stormwater flooding, and FEMA 100- and 500-year floodplains to identify areas and assets exposed to multiple flood hazards.



Flood Insurance & Repetitive Loss Analysis: Analyzed NFIP policy and claims data to examine flood insurance participation and patterns of repetitive flood losses.
Shoreline Change Analysis: Used historical National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP) aerial imagery to delineate shoreline positions and assess coastal erosion and accretion between 2007 and 2025. Calculated net shoreline movement and end point rate along transects to quantify the magnitude and rate of shoreline change.




Data:
County parcel data • NOAA sea level rise • SLOSH storm surge • NAIP Imagery


Application
These analyses support the city’s floodplain management planning by identifying areas vulnerable to flooding, examining insurance coverage and repetitive flood losses, and informing potential mitigation priorities.

Photo taken in Hattiesburg, MS during an EPA Brownfield Site Assessment “tank yank.”




I am a quantitative social scientist with a Ph.D. in Sociology from Louisiana State University, specializing in disaster research, geospatial analysis, and community resilience. My work examines how disasters and environmental risks affect communities, with particular attention to social inequality, housing, and recovery outcomes.
My research combines quantitative and spatial methods to investigate the social dimensions of disasters and climate change. Through my doctoral research, I examined how climate change attributable flooding from Hurricane Harvey influenced housing markets and flood insurance participation across neighborhoods with different socioeconomic characteristics.
Beyond academic research, I work with local governments along the Mississippi Gulf Coast to support flood risk assessments and resilience planning initiatives. This work brings together spatial analysis, local knowledge, and the practical challenges of planning for environmental change.

title: D’Iberville, MS | CRS Activity 610
text:
Overview
This project supported the City of D’Iberville in developing a flood response plan for FEMA’s Community Rating System (CRS) Activity 610.
My role was to characterize building exposure under coastal storm surge and riverine flood scenarios. Using R, I calculated the proportion of buildings exposed to different flooding conditions and used ArcGIS Pro to map flood extent, depth, affected structures, and overlap with the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA). The analysis incorporated NOAA riverine flood stages and hurricane storm surge scenarios to provide a consistent basis for evaluating flood exposure across the city.




My Role & Contributions

Flood Scenario Development: Evaluated Category 1 and Category 3 hurricane storm surge alongside minor, moderate, and major riverine flood stages.
Building Exposure Analysis: Integrated flood inundation data with building footprints to quantify the proportion of structures exposed under each scenario.
Critical Facilities Assessment: Geocoded and mapped critical facilities to support identification of potentially affected infrastructure.
Planning Coordination: Participated in stakeholder meetings to align flood scenarios with existing community forecasting and response protocols.

Data

Coastal scenarios: SLOSH
Riverine scenarios: NOAA Riverine Flood Inundation
Local building footprints



Application
The resulting maps and exposure estimates support scenario-based flood response planning by identifying where structures and critical facilities may be affected as flood conditions intensify.

title: Mapping Flood Insurance Participation
text:
This independent project uses publicly available National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) data to map residential flood insurance participation across coastal Mississippi at the census block group level.
By integrating NFIP policy records with U.S. Census housing data, the analysis examines the geographic distribution of flood insurance coverage and identifies communities with relatively low levels of participation. The project also demonstrates a reproducible workflow for accessing, processing, and visualizing federal flood insurance data.







Data
OpenFEMA NFIP Policies · U.S. Census/ACS housing data
Data & Reproducibility: View Project on Github.

title: Waveland, MS | CRS Activity 510
text:
Overview
This project supported the City of Waveland, Mississippi, in developing four planning documents under FEMA’s Community Rating System (CRS): a floodplain management plan, substantial damage management plan, repetitive loss area analysis, and natural floodplain functions plan.
The project brought together flood hazard, property, infrastructure, and insurance data to better understand the city’s flood risks and inform local floodplain management priorities.




My Role & Contributions
Community Planning & Engagement: Developed supporting maps and analyses, contributed to planning documents, and participated in stakeholder engagement to inform local floodplain management strategies.
Floodplain Management Plan

Multi-Hazard Exposure Assessment: Mapped storm surge, high-tide flooding, stormwater flooding, FEMA 100- and 500-year floodplains, and shoreline change to characterize the city’s exposure to multiple hazards.
Flood Insurance Analysis: Analyzed NFIP policy and claims data and identified patterns of insurance participation to support flood mitigation priorities.

Repetitive Loss Area Analysis

Repetitive Loss Area Delineation: Analyzed FEMA repetitive loss records and NFIP claims data to identify and map areas with concentrations of repetitive flood losses.

Substantial Damage Management Plan

Substantial Damage Assessment & Mapping: Identified and mapped properties potentially subject to substantial damage determinations and entered property information into FEMA’s Substantial Damage Estimator (SDE) tool.
SDE Guidance & Documentation: Developed a user guide to help municipal staff navigate the SDE tool and conduct substantial damage assessments.



Data
FEMA NFIP Claims & Policies • County parcel data • NOAA sea level rise and high tide flooding • SLOSH storm surge • MDEQ digital elevation model • USGS Shorelines • HUC watersheds


Application
Together, these analyses help the city identify areas most vulnerable to flooding, understand patterns of flood insurance participation and repetitive losses, and prioritize future flood mitigation efforts.
